quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

entry.rationale: The tree cites the 1860 U.S. Federal Census (S2) for the parent-child link from Thomas Flynn (I2) to Patrick Flynn (I1), but no assertion or log entry records what it shows. This household search tests whether Patrick (about 15) is still listed with Thomas and whether a wife is named. The 1860 census is name-searchable on FamilySearch.

Patrick (about 25) and Thomas Flynn (about 52) should both appear in 1870 if living. The household shows whether Patrick still lives with Thomas and may name Thomas's wife, the unknown mother. The 1870 census is name-searchable on FamilySearch and free, so it is searched before the paid Ancestry index.

Requested check of the 1870 federal census on Ancestry (paid index). Its transcription is independent of FamilySearch's, so it can confirm or correct the household members and the wife's name read in the sequence 2 item. Search Thomas and Patrick Flynn in Schuylkill County.

The parents' marriage is needed to confirm the couple as a unit and to name the mother, which census records omit. Thomas Flynn (born about 1818) would have married before Patrick's birth (about 1845). The county marriage index is name-searchable on FamilySearch. The marriage may have taken place in Ireland, so a negative result does not rule out a marriage.

Companion to the county marriage item: a Catholic church marriage register may hold the parents' marriage. Schuylkill parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia, so the register is held at the parish or diocese, not the county. Church Marriages 1682-1976 is name-searchable on FamilySearch.

If the 1860 or 1870 household shows Thomas with a wife who is not the mother of Patrick, or if her surname differs between records, she may have married before. Search Thomas Flynn's later marriages to find a prior marriage of the wife. The civil marriage collection is name-searchable on FamilySearch. This tests the surname given by one marriage record and does not settle her maiden name.

A will or administration for Thomas Flynn may name Patrick as a son and list the widow and heirs. The window runs from 1850 because Thomas would be about 32 then, and to 1900 because he could have died as late as age 80 (window set by Thomas's lifespan). The Schuylkill Register of Wills holds records from 1811, and the Pennsylvania probate collection is browse-only, so this is an image browse. A mortality schedule check for 1850-1880 is a companion test of an earlier death.

FAN item for the parentage question. Deeds in the Pennsylvania Wills and Deeds collection (name-searchable) for Thomas Flynn may name adjoining landowners who are kin, and a deed or estate sale may name Patrick or the widow. Boundary recitals name neighbours, who may be relatives of the wife.

Patrick's own burial entry, dated after his death on 1908-03-12 in Schuylkill County. The tree already cites a Pennsylvania death certificate (S3) for that death, so this item targets the burial record instead. Burial entries often state age, birthplace and parents' names. The cemetery collection is name-searchable on FamilySearch.

The objective states Patrick was born in Pennsylvania, but the tree and the 1850 census assertion give Ireland. This item tests the Pennsylvania birth claim in the Births and Christenings collection, which is name-searchable on FamilySearch. Pennsylvania records do not replace a birth in Ireland, so a negative result is informative.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1845-1908

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

entry.rationale: Pennsylvania Death Certificates, 1906-1968 is name-searchable and covers Patrick Flynn's death on 1908-03-12 in Schuylkill County, after statewide registration began in 1906. The tree cites S3 for that death fact, but no assertion from S3 is extracted and nothing in the project yet names his parents. Death certificates of this period often record the decedent's father and mother, so a certificate naming Thomas Flynn as father would be direct evidence for the link.

United States, Census, 1860 is name-searchable. The tree's parentage link cites S2 (1860 census), but no assertion from it has been extracted. The 1850 census (log_001) places Patrick, age 5, in Thomas Flynn's household. The 1860 household tests whether Patrick is still with Thomas at about age 15, whether the household names a wife, and who else lives there.

Dedicated parents' marriage item: the marriage of Thomas Flynn (b. about 1818, Ireland) to Patrick's mother. Pennsylvania Civil Marriages, 1677-1950 and Pennsylvania Compiled Marriages, 1700-1900 are name-searchable (loc_001). The marriage confirms the couple as a unit and may give the mother's maiden name, but only if it was her first marriage. Compare its date with Patrick's birth of about 1845. It does not by itself prove Patrick is their child.

Companion to the parents' marriage item: searches for any other marriage of Thomas Flynn, so that the wife named in Patrick's household is not assumed to be his first wife. Thomas's later marriages, if any, may name a different wife or a different surname for the mother. Pennsylvania Civil Marriages, 1677-1950 and Pennsylvania Compiled Marriages, 1700-1900 are name-searchable. No surname is assumed for the wife.

Family-associate (FAN) item: baptisms of Flynn children in Schuylkill County parishes, which name both parents directly. Sibling baptisms would confirm the same parents. Pennsylvania, Births and Christenings is name-searchable, and Schuylkill County Church Records is name-searchable (loc_001). Roman Catholic sacramental registers are held at the parish or diocese, not the county, so if an index entry is missing, browse the parish register images.

Pennsylvania Probate Records, 1683-1994 is browse-only (loc_001). Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811, and a will or administration of Thomas Flynn could name Patrick as a son. The window is set by Thomas's own lifespan (b. about 1818), not by the 1908 death of Patrick. Browse the Schuylkill Register of Wills images for a Flynn estate.

United States Census (Mortality Schedule), 1850-1880 is name-searchable. It tests whether Thomas Flynn died in the county in that span. A death there fixes the window for the probate and burial items. Mortality schedules record the decedent's age and place, which helps confirm identity against the 1850 household.

Pennsylvania Cemetery Records, ca. 1700-ca. 1950 and Pennsylvania Deaths and Burials, 1720-1999 are name-searchable. A burial entry for Thomas Flynn may give his age, birthplace and the name of a surviving wife. The window runs to 1908 so that a burial after Patrick's own death is covered.

Patrick Flynn's own marriage, if one exists in the county. The marriage record may name his father and mother, and the groom's parents are a separate line of evidence from his death certificate. Pennsylvania Compiled Marriages, 1700-1900 and Pennsylvania Civil Marriages, 1677-1950 are name-searchable (loc_001).

Patrick's birthplace is Ireland (1850 census, log_001), and the origin baptism is not name-indexed, so indexed search on the surname will not reach it. Run a full-text co-occurrence search for Thomas Flynn and the mother's name as separate terms in parish registers, unscoped to a collection. Run this once items 1 to 9 have produced a county or parish of origin or a mother's name, so the search has a target. Priests may reverse or conflate the parents' names, so treat which name is the father's as unsettled.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

Patrick's baptism may name Thomas Flynn as father and the mother by maiden name. The tree gives his birth as ~1845 in Ireland, but the objective says Pennsylvania, and the 1850 census gives the birthplace as Ireland. items.question: Besides Mary, John, Rebecca, William and Joseph, who were the other children of Thomas Hale (b. about 1810, Pennsylvania; d. 1868, Greene County, Ohio) and his wife Sarah?
items.rationale: Primary research objective. The tree holds the couple and five children; no records have been searched yet for any others.

entry.rationale: The tree holds Thomas Hale (birth about 1810, Pennsylvania; death 1868, Greene County) and Sarah Hale, with Mary (birth about 1836), John (about 1838), Rebecca (about 1841), William (about 1844) and Joseph (about 1847), all recorded as born in Greene County. The 1850 census names every household member with an age, so it is the first test of which other children were living at home. The United States Census, 1850 collection is name-searchable.

Second household listing with Thomas still alive. Children born 1836 to 1847 would be roughly 13 to 24, and any child born after 1847 would appear for the first time. Comparing it with the 1850 listing shows any child who left or died in between. The United States Census, 1860 collection is name-searchable.
Thomas died in 1868 per the tree, so the 1870 household is Sarah's and shows any younger children still living with her as a widow. The United States Census, 1870 collection is name-searchable.
If Sarah was still living in 1880, this household shows any unmarried child at home with her. The United States Census, 1880 collection is name-searchable.

Baptism records name both parents and often list siblings born in the same parish. The Ohio, Church and Civil Births and Baptisms collection is name-searchable, and the wider Ohio, Church Records collection is name-searchable as well. A baptism of an unlisted child would show a family member the census listings missed.

Ohio births before statewide civil registration in 1867 are largely absent from state registration, so the Ohio, Births and Christenings collection, which is name-searchable, is the route to birth entries for children born in Greene County from 1836 onward. A birth entry naming Thomas and Sarah as parents would confirm an additional child.

The marriage of Thomas Hale and Sarah, probably before Mary's birth about 1836, dates the start of the family and may give Sarah's maiden name, which the tree does not hold. The Ohio, County Marriages collection is name-searchable. Later marriages of the children in the same collection may name the parents and list siblings.

Thomas died in 1868 in Greene County, and a death or burial entry, or an obituary, may list surviving children by name. The Ohio, Deaths and Burials collection, 1854 to 1997, is name-searchable. Sarah's death entry, if it falls in the same range, serves the same purpose.

Thomas's estate, opened after his 1868 death, would be filed with the Greene County Probate Court, which took over from the Court of Common Pleas in 1852. Administration papers and an heirs' list commonly name each surviving child. The Ohio, Probate Records collection is browse-only, so this is an image browse of the Greene County files. The window extends to 1900 to cover Sarah's estate, since she could have died well after 1868.

Deeds made by heirs after Thomas died, such as sales or partitions of his land, name each child as a grantor. The Ohio, Wills and Deeds collection is name-searchable. It is a fallback for the probate item if the estate file is missing or lacks an heirs' list.

items.guide_markdown:
## Baiersbronn, Württemberg - 1800s

Church books are on Archion (parish page above).

entry.rationale: Katharina was born about 1843 in Baiersbronn. A Protestant baptism entry should name her father and mother, the most direct route to the parents. The locality entry says the Baiersbronn church books are digitised on Archion, not FamilySearch, and no FamilySearch collection for the place was returned, so this is a manual hand-off to the researcher. The window starts a few years before the estimated birth to allow for the year's uncertainty.

Dedicated search for the parents' marriage in the Baiersbronn Protestant marriage register. It confirms the couple as a unit, may give the mother's maiden name, and its date relative to the about-1843 birth corroborates any father found elsewhere. It does not by itself prove Katharina is their child. The tree records no marriage for any candidate parent, so the search is keyed on the surname once a baptism or other record names the parents. If the mother married more than once, her other marriage entries must also be checked before her maiden name is taken as settled.

Burial and death entries for the parents, and the Familienregister, which may list the household's children with dates. They are the fallback if the baptism entry is missing, and they can name the parents' ages and parish. Dated after the birth so the parents' death is searched after the child was born.

Katharina's own marriage entry. The locality entry gives no register start date, so the baptism may be out of reach. A marriage entry usually states the bride's age, home parish and parents' names, and is a route to her origin if the baptism is missing.

FAN search: baptisms and marriages of Seeger siblings and godparents in the same register. A sibling's baptism names the same parents, and a godparent's entry may show the family's kin. This is the parentage FAN item the question requires, and it also serves as a fallback if the subject's own baptism is not in the register.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

It will look at the marriage records of Thomas Flynn and of Patrick, the probate and deed files, the neighbors in the 1850 and 1860 censuses, the 1870, 1880 and 1900 censuses, cemetery burials, and baptisms of Patrick's siblings.

The next step is to search the 1835-1846 marriage records for Thomas Flynn, because a marriage record there could name Patrick's mother and open the rest of the search.

The County Marriages and Civil Marriages collections are name-searchable. It does not by itself show that Patrick is their child; item 3 and the FAN items carry that test.

Remarriage check for Thomas Flynn. A surname given in the item 1 marriage record may be a prior married name, so this searches any later marriage of Thomas, which could name a different wife and the mother's maiden name. Same name-searchable County Marriages and Civil Marriages collections, read against item 1.

Direct parentage test that pl_002 left unsearched: a will or administration of Thomas Flynn naming Patrick as a son would settle the question. Its heirs and widow list is also FAN evidence, naming the mother and other children. Probate records are held by the county Register of Wills from 1811 (loc_001). The Pennsylvania Probate Records collection is browse-only, so this is an image browse of the county dockets, not a name search. The window is sized to Thomas's possible lifespan (born ~1818, death plausibly 1850-1900), not to Patrick's research window.

FAN neighbors of the 1850 Thomas Flynn household (dwelling 84, family 91). Patrick is recorded in that household, but no record states their relationship. Browsing the dwellings either side can show Irish-born families, a widow or kinsman who shares a surname with the mother, or Flynn relatives living close by. The 1850 Flynn household itself was searched under pl_001, so this item covers the neighbors only. The 1850 census is name-searchable nationally, but neighbors can only be reached by image browse.

FAN neighbors of the 1860 Thomas Flynn household (dwelling 112, family 119). Same purpose as item 4, for the decade when Patrick was about 15. Adjacent dwellings may show a kinsman or an in-law household, and the image browse shows who lived beside the family. The 1860 Flynn household was searched under pl_002, so this covers the neighbors only.

Gap listed in ps_001: the 1870 census has not been searched. Search for the Thomas Flynn household and for Patrick (about 25) to test whether he is still living with Thomas, and record the other members. Co-residents and the household's neighbors are FAN leads to the mother's family. The 1870 census is name-searchable nationally.

Gap listed in ps_001: the 1880 census has not been searched. The 1880 schedule is the first to state each person's relationship to the head of household and the birthplaces of each person's parents. Gap listed in ps_001: the 1900 census has not been searched. A sibling's baptism or christening names both parents, and so may give the mother's name directly; sponsors are FAN leads. The Pennsylvania Births and Christenings collection is name-searchable. Patrick's own marriage record, a FAN source. A marriage record can name the groom's parents, and the bondsmen, witnesses and bride's family often include kin. The County Marriages and Civil Marriages collections are name-searchable.

FAN land search: Schuylkill County deeds and wills where Thomas Flynn is grantor, grantee or witness. Adjoining landowners named in a boundary recital are neighbors by definition and are often kin. A deed conveying land to Patrick would also be direct parentage evidence. The Pennsylvania Wills and Deeds collection is name-searchable.

FAN cemetery search: burials of Thomas Flynn, the mother, and any Flynn relatives in Schuylkill County cemeteries. items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1870-1882

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.

Neighbours enumerated alongside the Flynns can be kin, sponsors or lodgers who speak to Patrick's parentage, and the enumerator's order shows which households the Flynns lived among. United States, Census, 1850 is name-searchable, but neighbours are reached by browsing the page images.

The tree attaches the Pennsylvania death certificate (S3) to Patrick's death fact (1908-03-12, Schuylkill County) but records no content from it. Read the certificate itself for the parents' names it gives, since Pennsylvania statewide death registration began in 1906 and this is the one record that names parents for the death year. The tree's parent-child link already cites S3, so this item tests that citation rather than assuming it.

If Thomas Flynn (born about 1818, Ireland) died in Schuylkill County, his will or administration would name his children, Patrick among them. The date window is sized to Thomas's plausible lifespan, not to Patrick's. Probate records from 1811 are held by the Schuylkill County Register of Wills; the FamilySearch image group for Schuylkill probate, 1851-1930, is browse-only, so this is an image browse of the dockets.

Fallback for the probate item. The Schuylkill Orphans' Court holds estate dockets, distributions and guardianships, which can name heirs when the Register of Wills file is missing or not indexed. Guardianship or distribution papers naming a minor Patrick would be direct parentage evidence.

Follows the household forward. The 1870 and 1880 federal censuses are name-searchable. The 1880 schedule states relationship to head, so it can confirm Patrick as Thomas's son or show Patrick's mother's household after Thomas's death. Patrick would be 25 to 35 in these years.

The record supplies the mother's maiden name, which the census and death records usually omit, and dates the couple's union against Patrick's birth. A marriage proves the couple married, not that Patrick is their child. Search every marriage of the mother, not only the one to Thomas, because a remarriage would make the surname on any one record unreliable. The first marriage may have been in Ireland, outside this locality, which needs its own survey before it can be planned.

Thomas Flynn's burial, if he died in the county, would give his death date and an age from which his birth year can be checked. Pennsylvania Cemetery Records (1700-1950) is name-searchable. A burial can also name a spouse or child as the informant, which bears on the household.

From the tree and the log: Martha J Neal (I2) is recorded as born about 1859 in Georgia. She appears under three married surnames: Neal (her 31 Jul 1879 Hill County, Texas marriage to James M Neal, log_001), Landham (the widow's styling on that record, with no prior marriage found), and Hamby (a later 1888 marriage). Her earliest marriage found so far is the 7 Jan 1869 Smith County marriage of W F Lanham to "M J Wood" (log_002), but nothing yet shows it was her first. The pre-existing tree source placing an "M M Wood" household in the 1860 Blount County, Alabama census is uncited and unconfirmed. No parent is recorded for her in the tree.

Plan items in execution order:
- pli_001, census, Blount County, Alabama, 1860, FamilySearch: test the "M M Wood" household for a child of about one and the neighbouring households.
- pli_002, vital record, Blount County, Alabama, 1845-1869, FamilySearch full-text: any Wood bride's marriage before 1869, which would be her first and would give her birth surname.
- pli_003, vital record, Blount County, Alabama, 1845-1859, FamilySearch full-text: the candidate parents' marriage to each other. If they married in Georgia, this item cannot reach it.
- pli_004, vital record, Smith County, Texas, 1869, FamilySearch full-text: FAN on the 1869 Lanham marriage bondsman and witnesses.
- pli_005, census, Smith County, Texas, 1870, FamilySearch: the W F Lanham household, to test whether the 1869 bride is Martha.
- pli_006, vital record, Hill County, Texas, 1880-1889, FamilySearch: the 1888 Hamby marriage, which may name her as a widow under a prior surname.
- pli_007, church, Blount County, Alabama, 1855-1875, FamilySearch: baptisms of Wood children naming parents.
- pli_008, probate, Blount County, Alabama, 1859-1919, FamilySearch full-text keyword search: a Wood estate naming Martha or a daughter as heir.
- pli_009, cemetery, Texas, 1888-1930, FamilySearch: Martha's own death or burial entry, which may state her age, birthplace or parents.

Two gaps to flag. First, the Georgia birthplace has no locality entry, so no Georgia items are planned. A Georgia locality survey is needed before any search of the parents' Georgia records. Second, the pli_009 jurisdiction is left at state level until the 1888 marriage shows where she lived.

The next step is to run the Blount County 1860 census check (pli_001) and the Alabama marriage search (pli_002), since they decide whether the Wood lead is hers.

items.rationale: Test the pre-existing tree source that places an 'M M Wood' household in the 1860 census of Blount County (volume 005154190, 99% name-indexed, per loc_001). Martha's birth year (about 1859) and Georgia birthplace fit, but the tree source is uncited and the name is not confirmed as hers. The household shows whether a child of about one sits with a Wood couple, which is the direct test of parentage. Read the neighbouring households too, as FAN sources. The 1860 federal census is name-searchable.

Find any marriage of a Wood bride (M J or Martha) in Blount County before the 7 Jan 1869 Smith County marriage to W F Lanham (log_002). The Alabama county marriage volumes 1820-1888 (volumes 007316661-007316663, 80-100% name-indexed, per loc_001) are the place to look, with the Alabama County Marriages collections as name-searchable backup. A pre-1869 Wood marriage would be her first, so its bride surname is her birth name, and the record may name her father. A Wood marriage found only after 1869 would not be her first.

Dedicated search for the marriage of the candidate Wood parents to each other, which would confirm the couple as a unit and give the mother's maiden name. Use the Alabama county marriage volumes 1820-1888 (per loc_001). This marriage does not by itself prove that Martha is their child, and the link must come from a record placing her with them (items 1 and 7). If the couple married in Georgia, where Martha was reportedly born, this item cannot reach that marriage and a Georgia locality survey is needed first.

FAN item on the 7 Jan 1869 Smith County marriage of W F Lanham and M J Wood (log_002, a_004). The bondsman, witnesses and officiant on that record may be Wood kin or neighbours who speak to the bride's origin. The Smith County marriage volumes 1857-1876 (volumes 007255720-007255721) are 100% name-indexed and full-text searchable (loc_002). A bondsman sharing the Wood surname would point back to the family in Alabama.

Find the W F Lanham household in the 1870 census. It should show a wife whose age and birthplace can be checked against the about-1859 Georgia estimate. It tests whether the M J Wood of 1869 is the same woman as Martha, and whether a Wood relative or a child appears in the household. The 1870 federal census is name-searchable (nationalCollections, United States, Census, 1870).

Find the 1888 marriage of Martha to Hamby, the later marriage (q_002 rationale). The Texas Marriages collection (1837-1973) is name-searchable and covers Hill and Smith Counties (loc_002). A Hamby marriage record may name her as a widow under a prior surname, and may give her parents or the prior husband, which narrows the earlier marriage in item 2.

Search for baptisms of Wood children in Blount County, which would name the parents and the child's birth date. Alabama Church Records 1831-1994 is name-searchable (loc_001). Because the register start date for the parish is not in the locality entry, this is a check on whether a baptism survives, not an assumed source. A baptism naming Martha or her siblings would test the 1860 census household.

Keyword search of Alabama probate records (1809-1985, browse-only; per loc_001 full-text but not name-indexed) for a Wood estate that names Martha, M J, or a daughter as heir. The window runs from her birth to a father's plausible death, since the creator's lifespan sets the bounds. This is a keyword search, not a name search, because the collection is not name-indexed.

Martha's own death or burial entry. Her birth window (about 1859, Georgia) predates any register this question can reach in the Alabama and Texas parishes, so her death or burial record may state her age, birthplace or parents. The Texas Deaths and Burials (1903-1973) and Texas Death Index collections are name-searchable (loc_002), and the Hamby surname from her 1888 marriage is the search key. The jurisdiction is left at state level until item 6 names the county where she died.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

entry.rationale: Proof ps_001 rests on the 1850 and 1860 censuses, which state no relationships. The 1880 census is the first to give each member's relation to the head, so it can show whether Patrick is Thomas Flynn's son. The United States, Census, 1880 collection is name-searchable.

The 1870 census (United States, Census, 1870, name-searchable) is an open gap in ps_001. It may show Thomas's household, his wife's name and any siblings not seen in 1850 or 1860. It states no relationships, so it supports household continuity rather than parentage on its own.

The 1900 census (United States, Census, 1900, name-searchable) is an open gap in ps_001. It states relationships and gives Patrick's birth month and year and his parents' birthplaces. It tests the Ireland versus Pennsylvania birthplace conflict recorded in ps_001 and may show whether Thomas is still living.

Dedicated parentage item for the candidate parents' marriage to each other. The County Marriages and Church Marriages collections for Pennsylvania are name-searchable. A marriage before Patrick's birth confirms the couple as a unit and may give the mother's maiden name, if this was her first marriage. If the marriage took place in Ireland, this search will not reach it. That would need an Irish locality survey.

Patrick's own marriage. The County Marriages collection is name-searchable. A marriage record gives the names of the bride's and groom's parents in many cases, so it may name Thomas Flynn and the mother. It is a second route to parentage that does not depend on the census.

Remarriage check. The 1850 and 1860 censuses do not name Thomas's wife, and a surname given on one marriage record may not be her birth name. Search County Marriages for any later marriage of Thomas Flynn's widow or of Thomas himself. Its result tests whether the mother named in the parents' marriage was her first marriage. The search runs on the surname only as a lead and claims nothing about her maiden name.

Thomas Flynn was born about 1818, so his probate file can fall anywhere from about 1850 to 1910. The Register of Wills held probate from 1811. The Pennsylvania, Probate Records collection is browse-only, so this is an image browse of the Schuylkill docket. A will or administration naming Patrick as a son would be direct parentage evidence.

Thomas Flynn's death and burial entries, and his wife's, can state an age, a birthplace or a parish. The Pennsylvania Deaths and Burials and Cemetery Records collections are name-searchable. This is the main route to the birthplace of the parents, given that no Irish baptism is in reach.

FAN item. James Brown, who informed Patrick's death certificate, was Patrick's son-in-law. His marriage to a Flynn daughter, in the County Marriages collection (name-searchable), names her parents and so may name Thomas Flynn and the mother as the daughter's parents. It is a sibling link that does not depend on Patrick's own records.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.guide_markdown:
## Stagstrup Sogn, Thisted Amt, Denmark - late 1700s

For a male subject born 1779, two record classes carry parentage. Church books (kirkeboeger) hold the baptism naming both parents. The military levy rolls (laegdsruller), kept from 1789, enroll every boy under his father's name from childhood - direct evidence of the father. Danish patronymics (Nielsen = son of Niels) point to the father's given name but not the specific man. The Stagstrup register is only ~3% indexed, so plan to browse images.

entry.rationale: The baptism of Mikkel Nielsen Blyeberg (born 20 Aug 1779) in the Stagstrup church book is the primary parentage record, since Danish baptism entries name both parents. The Stagstrup kirkebog image group is browse-only and only about 3% name-indexed (loc_001), so the register must be browsed by year from 1779. The patronymic Nielsen points to a father named Niels but not which Niels, so the entry must be read for the father's full name.

entry.jurisdiction: Thisted Amt (Vestervig and Thisted districts), Denmark
entry.repository: FamilySearch (name-searchable collection 2513529; browse-only Thisted districts image group)
entry.rationale: Levy rolls (laegdsruller) begin in 1789 and enrol each boy under his father's name from early childhood (loc_001 quirk). A roll entry for Mikkel placed directly beneath his father is direct parentage evidence for a male subject born 1779. Search the name-searchable collection first; if it does not show the entry, browse the browse-only Thisted districts image group, following the boy's supplemental number across parish moves.

The 1787 Danish census is the earliest household listing and falls when Mikkel was about seven. If the household at Stagstrup lists a Niels with a son Mikkel, that co-residence corroborates the father named by the baptism or levy roll. Co-residence alone does not establish parentage, so this item only corroborates.

A dedicated item for the candidate parents' marriage to each other. The marriage in the Stagstrup church book, browsed for the years before the 1779 birth, confirms the couple as a unit and, if it was the mother's first marriage, supplies her maiden name, which census and death records usually omit. Because a remarriage is possible, any marriage record naming her must be checked, not only the first. The marriage dates the union but does not by itself prove the child is theirs.

FAN item: baptisms of Mikkel's siblings and the godparents named in them, in the same Stagstrup register. A sibling's baptism naming the same parents, or a godparent who is a paternal relative, can confirm the father's name independently of Mikkel's own entry. Naming customs in loc_001 and the Denmark Naming Customs page (first son named for the father's father) help identify the grandfather and any uncle among the godparents.

Once the father's full name is known, his burial in the Stagstrup church book gives his death date, which the objective also requires. Burials in this register are browse-only and unindexed, so the register is read by year after the father's name is fixed. Sequenced after the baptism because the burial is searched by the name the baptism supplies.

entry.repository: FamilySearch (name-searchable collection 2015318; browse-only Hassing Herred image group)
entry.rationale: Probate estate records (skifteprotokoller) for the father, where the dates run from his likely death through the decades after it. A probate file can name Mikkel as a son and give the father's death date. The window is sized to the father's own lifespan, not the subject's, because the father, not Mikkel, is the creator of the estate file. Fallback if the church burial is not found.

## Lincolnshire, England - 1750-1800

FamilySearch's 'England, Births and Christenings' collection (1473014) is a partial Legacy index: it does not index all records for this place or period, and no records or corrections are being added — a nil there is a statement about the index, not proof that no christening exists; search the parish register itself before concluding absence. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/England,_Births_and_Christenings_-_FamilySearch_Historical_Records)

entry.rationale: Mary Dawson's christening, about 1772 birth, should name her parents. The locality entry lists England, Births and Christenings, 1538-1975 (collection 1473014) as name-searchable, but it is a partial Legacy index with no additions or corrections. Search Mary Dawson under variant forms (Mary, Mari, Polly) with the father's name blank. A nil result is a statement about the index only, not proof that no christening exists.

Fallback for item 1. If the partial index gives no Dawson christening, browse the Lincolnshire parish baptism registers for the parish where Dawson families are found, because the register itself settles whether the entry exists. The parish is not yet known, so this depends on names and places found in item 1 or item 7.

Parents' marriage, a dedicated parentage item. It would confirm the candidate parents as a couple, date their union against Mary's birth about 1772, and give the mother's maiden name only if this was her first marriage. Her other marriages are unknown, so a surname here may be a later married name, not her birth name. Marriage alone does not prove Mary is their child; a record placing her with them is still needed.

Mary's own marriage. Parish marriage registers from 1754 often name the bride's father, and this may state him directly. Her birth parish is unknown, so search the Lincolnshire marriage registers and browse images where no name index covers the parish.

Mary's own burial or death entry. It states an age and sometimes a birthplace or parish, which can point back to her origin where a baptism is not found, since the baptism register start for her parish is not yet known.

Friends-and-neighbours item for parentage. Baptisms of Mary's siblings, naming the same parents, and godparent entries in the same parish, can establish the family unit and the parents' names. Search the surname Dawson across Lincolnshire baptisms in the same years.

A father's will or administration naming Mary as a daughter is direct parentage evidence. The window is sized to a father of a child born about 1772, who could die anywhere from then to about 1830, not to the subject's own lifespan. The Lincolnshire probate series is not yet confirmed as name-searchable; verify its access before relying on it.

## Württemberg, Germany - 1780-1830

German children baptised with two or more given names were often called by the second in daily life (the wiki's example: Johann Christoph and Johann Friedrich were usually called Christoph and Friedrich) — search later records under the second given name alone as well as the full baptismal name. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Germany_Naming_Customs)

Search under Anna Margaretha and under Margaretha alone, because the locality entry notes that German children were often called by their second given name. The entry gives no register start date for the parish, so whether this baptism survives is untested.

Dedicated item for the parents' marriage. Germany Marriages, 1558-1929 (collection 1473009) is name-searchable per the locality entry. It is keyed on the father's surname once item 1 names him, since a given name and parish alone do not identify the couple. The marriage supplies the mother's maiden name only if it was her first marriage. Its date before the 1792 birth corroborates a father named by other evidence. It does not by itself show that Anna is their child.

Fan item: baptisms of Anna's siblings and of the godparents in the same parish, from Germany, Births and Baptisms, 1558-1898 (collection 1473000, name-searchable). A sibling's baptism names the same parents, and the sponsors show the family's kin network. This is the fallback if item 1 does not yield the parents' names, since a sibling baptism names the same parents.

Anna's own marriage record. Germany Marriages, 1558-1929 (collection 1473009, name-searchable) may name her father, and sometimes her mother, as well as her home parish. Search under both given names, per the second-name practice in the locality entry.

Anna's burial entry. Burial registers often state age, home parish and sometimes parents' names, which matters because the birth register may not hold her baptism. The collection for burials is not confirmed by a tool call in this session, so confirm its availability before searching.

If Anna's father died while she was a minor, a probate or guardianship file would name the children and their mother. The window runs from the 1792 birth to the end of a father born about 1750-1770, which sets the creator's plausible death years, not Anna's. The records sit with the Württemberg state archives. The item is not name-searchable, so the search is a browse of the file, and it depends on the father's name from item 1.

items.guide_markdown:
## Locality Guide: Trysil, Hedmark, Norway (1780–1880)

### Jurisdictional Context

Trysil became its own *prestegjeld* in 1780, separated from Elverum. The 1860 death falls squarely within Trysil's own records. Administratively: Amt of Hedmark from 1781; Sorenskriveri of Søndre Østerdalen; Diocese of Oslo/Christiania 1537–1864, then Hamar.

### Church Records — Primary Source

- **Digitized images** (browse-only, 0% name-indexed): Kirkebøker 1588–1928 (Trysil prestegjeld) at FamilySearch Catalog (cat. 737) and Digitalarkivet. The 1860 burial will be in volume 008679203_003 (1814–1877, 325 images).
- **Indexed national extracts** (name-searchable): Norway Burials 1666–1927 (FS col 1468081; also Ancestry, MyHeritage); Norway Baptisms 1634–1927 (FS col 1467014); Norway Marriages 1660–1926 (FS col 1468080).
- **Dissenter church**: Trysil Frimenighet 1858–1920 at Digitalarkivet (images).

### Census

| Year | FS Collection | Access | Notes |
|------|--------------|--------|-------|
| 1801 | 3733603 | indexed & images | Subject ~21; also Ancestry, MyHeritage |
| 1865 | 3756102 | indexed & images | Postdates death; shows widow/children |
| 1870 | 4135961 | indexed & images | Postdates death |
| 1875 | 1529106 | indexed & images | Postdates death; also Ancestry, MyHeritage |

### Probate

- Norway Probate Index Cards 1640–1903 (FS col 1661306): indexed — locate the 1860 estate filing here.
- Skifteprotokoller image volumes at FS Catalog cover through 1853; post-1853 volumes held at Riksarkivet/Digitalarkivet.

### Land Records

- Pantebøker (mortgage/property) 1712–1860 (FS Catalog 489152) — images.

### Military / Levy Rolls

Norway's conscription/levy rolls (*lægdsruller*) began 1789. Each enrolled boy is listed under his father's name — direct parentage evidence. A male born ~1780 would appear from approximately 1789. Access via Riksarkivet and Digitalarkivet.

### Farm Books (*Bygdebøker*)

Trysilboka (Lillevold, Larsen, Bryn; FS Library 948.23/T2 D2l) — multiple volumes covering farm histories and resident genealogies for Trysil with personal name indexes in volumes 1–3, 7–8. High-value source for locating a household at the farm level.

### Key Access Points

- **FamilySearch** (free): indexed burials/baptisms/marriages/census, browse church record images
- **Digitalarkivet** (free): church books at media.digitalarkivet.no/en/kb/browse
- **Ancestry** (subscription): Norway Burials/Baptisms/Marriages extracts, 1865 census
- **MyHeritage** (subscription): Norway Burials/Marriages, 1865/1875 census
- **FamilySearch Library** (on-site or center): Trysilboka farm book, catalog microfilm

items.guide_markdown:
## Kongsberg Parish, Buskerud, Norway — Locality Guide (1760–1810)

**Ecclesiastical jurisdiction:** Kongsberg prestegjeld, Kongsberg prosti, Oslo bispedømme (until 1948). Civil jurisdiction in 1780: Buskerud amt (from 1680), Numedal og Sandsvær sorenskriveri, Kongsberg Byfogderi (probate/skifterett).

### Church Records

All Kongsberg church record volumes at FamilySearch are **browse-only** (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable). Browse image by image.

**Key FamilySearch volumes for a ~1780 baptism:**
- **008680156_003** (1769–1782, 382 images) — prime target for a ~1780 birth
- **008680157_002** (1783–1797, 249 images) — wider date window fallback
- **008680157_003** (1795–1816, 380 images)
- **009061212** (Kongsberg + Jondalen combined, 1696–1915, 691 images)

**National indexed extracts (searchable):**
- Norway Baptisms 1634–1927 (FS col 1467014): 28,370 Kongsberg records — search first; coverage of 1780s may be incomplete
- Norway Marriages 1660–1926 (FS col 1468080)
- Norway Burials 1666–1927 (FS col 1468081)
- Same extracts also at Ancestry (Norway Select Baptisms col 60092) and MyHeritage

**Digitalarkivet:** Complete parish register scans 1696–1969 at media.digitalarkivet.no (Buskerud county, Kongsberg prestegjeld). Both Kongsberg proper and Jondalen sub-parish registers are available. Same material as FS volumes; browse by year range.

### Census Records
- 1801 census (FS col 3733603, indexed + images; also Digitalarkivet, Ancestry, MyHeritage)
- No pre-1801 national census; the mine rolls below partially fill this gap

### Kongsberg Sølvverk (Silver Mine) Records
Special census-type rolls at Digitalarkivet for mine employees:
- Pensjonister (pensioners) 1711; Borgere (citizens/residents) 1723; Funksjonærer (officials) 1765
These predate the ~1780 birth but may document a father employed at the mine.

### Military / Conscription (Lægdsruller)
Norwegian levy rolls began 1789. A male born ~1780 enrolled ~age 7–9, listed directly **under his father's name** — direct parentage evidence. Access: Digitalarkivet (browse and search) and Riksarkivet physical holdings for Numedal og Sandsvær lægd.

### Probate Records
- Kongsberg Byfogderi Skifteprotokoller 1739–1851 (FS Catalog 437559, browse-only; also Digitalarkivet)
- Norway Probate Index Cards 1640–1903 (FS col 1661306, indexed)
- Kongsberg deanery probate 1741–1816 at Digitalarkivet

### Land and Property
- Pantebøker (mortgage books) 1721–1864 at FamilySearch Catalog (no. 485469, Kongsberg Byfogderi)

The bride's earlier marriages are not known, so this item is paired with item 5 and with the census items above, which name the wife. items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1840-1900

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.
